amendments.rule: A repeated or resumptive element that the ASV renders once is still its own unit. Mark the unrepresented occurrence `unrepresented` rather than folding it into the rendered one. Where the repetition is a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral — Hebrew writes one `שָׁנָה` per numeral group where the ASV writes a single *years* — the rendered occurrence is the last, closing the whole Hebrew figure as the English noun closes the whole English one. Do not settle it by number agreement: Hebrew writes `שָׁנִים` after 2–10 and `שָׁנָה` from 11 up whatever the total, while the English plural follows the sum, so a match between them is an accident of two unrelated agreement systems and is not evidence. Do not settle it by which numeral the English noun stands beside either, since English drives the counted noun to the end of the phrase whatever order the translation chose. Tail-to-tail is what survives, and it holds across both Hebrew group orders and the ASV's frequent reordering of them. The genealogies are where this recurs, and BSB, which attaches the noun to its own phrase, disagrees on every first occurrence. **Tail-to-tail governs a run of absolute occurrences only.** Where the phrase is instead headed by a **construct** — a regnal date such as `בִּשְׁנַת עֶשְׂרִים וָשֶׁבַע שָׁנָה` → *In the twenty and seventh year* — the construct is what the English realizes, and the trailing absolute is the resumptive occurrence that goes `unrepresented`. So the rendered occurrence is the last of several absolutes but the first where a construct heads them, and MACULA's morphology is what decides which case this is. Position is the consequence, not the rule. **But a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused English word is not an unrendered occurrence.** Where a relative clause resumes its antecedent with a pronominal suffix on a preposition, or with a resumptive adverb, and the ASV writes one pronominal adverb for the whole — *wherein*, *whereon*, *whereby*, *whither*, and the bare *therein* of a preposition and its own suffix — the relative, the preposition and the resumptive morpheme share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, or on the preposition where no relative stands. Do not mark the suffix `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence: rule 30's one-English-word condition is met, because that word carries the resumption as well as the relation, exactly as *Nor* carries both the coordination and the negation in rule 35. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ` → *wherein* as one three-morpheme unit in twenty-one places and `בָּהּ` → *therein* as one two-morpheme unit in sixty-one, and records no unit where such a suffix stands outside the word. So ask first whether the English word carries the morpheme's sense: what this rule's first sentence governs is an element the ASV has left unwritten, as a second `בֵּין` or a surplus `שָׁנָה` is, and not one it has written inside a fusion. **The interrogative `אֵי` with a following `זֶה` is one interrogative expression, and its demonstrative is not an unrendered occurrence either.** Where the ASV renders `אֵי־זֶה` by a single interrogative word — *where*, *what*, *which* — the two morphemes share one unit under rule 30, headed on `אֵי`, which carries the wh-lexeme; the demonstrative is enclitic to the compound rather than a repeated or resumptive element, so this rule's first sentence does not reach it and it is never marked `unrepresented` beside a rendered `אֵי`. A construction-supplied copula joining that unit does not defeat rule 30's one-rendering condition, exactly as it does not for `לִפְנֵי` → *was before*, so `אֵי־זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ` → ***Where is*** *the way* fuses as `אֵי־זֶה` → *what* does. The corpus fuses this compound in every unit it records — JER.6.16, 1KI.13.12, ISA.66.1 twice, ECC.11.6 and 1KI.22.24 — and splits it in none. Two limits. Where the ASV spends a word on each morpheme, the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits them as usual. And this governs `אֵי־זֶה` and no other pair: a deictic `זֶה` standing after an interrogative that keeps its own English word — the `זֶה` of `לָמָּה זֶּה` or of `בֶּן־מִי־זֶה`, and the `זֶה` of `מִי זֶה` where the ASV writes *this* for it — is this rule's ordinary case, rendered where the ASV writes a word for it and `unrepresented` where it does not. **A resumptive possessive suffix is read on exactly those terms, and it need not stand on a preposition.** Where the clause resumes its antecedent with a suffix on a noun inside it and the ASV writes one *whose* for the pair, the relative and that suffix share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, while the noun keeps its own English: `אֶרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אֲבָנֶיהָ בַרְזֶל` → *a land* ***whose*** *stones are iron* is one unit on `אֲשֶׁר` and the suffix, with *stones* left to `אֶבֶן`. Contiguity is not the condition, for the reason rule 35 gives: however much of the clause stands between them, the one English word still carries both the relation and the resumption, so nothing is left over to mark. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר` with its resumptive suffix as one *whose* unit at DEU.28.49 and 1KI.8.39, and as a `noncompositional` one at AMO.2.9 and DAN.10.1 among eighteen such places. **But read which morphemes stand in each clause before counting a second occurrence.** Where a further clause is coordinated under the one written relative and the ASV rewrites its *whose* at the head of that clause, a resumptive suffix standing in that clause is what the second word realizes, under rule 18's sentence giving a suffix the English relative pronoun that renders it: `וּמֵהֲרָרֶיהָ תַּחְצֹב נְחֹשֶׁת` → *and out of* ***whose*** *hills thou mayest dig copper* gives its *whose* to the suffix on `הֲרָרֶיהָ`, not to the relative as a repetition under rule 25. Where no such suffix stands in the coordinated clause, rule 55's distributed subordinator governs as before and every occurrence is the relative's. **And read whether the suffix points at the antecedent at all before treating it as resumptive.** Every fusion above rests on a morpheme that resumes the antecedent, and a pronominal suffix standing inside the relative clause does that only where its referent is the antecedent; agreement is the first check and reference decides, so read MACULA's person, gender and number against the noun the clause modifies. Where the suffix instead denotes something else the clause speaks of, the one English pronominal adverb carries the relative's own relation and nothing of that suffix, rule 30's condition is unmet for it, and the fusion does not reach it: the relative takes the adverb alone, the suffix takes whatever English pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and the preposition it stands on is disposed of by rules 11 and 40 like any other. `וְאֶת־תַּחֲלֻאֶיהָ אֲשֶׁר־חִלָּה יְהוָה בָּהּ` → *and the sicknesses* ***wherewith*** *Jehovah hath made* ***it*** *sick* gives *wherewith* to `אֲשֶׁר` alone, *it* to the suffix of `בָּהּ`, which is feminine singular and denotes the land rather than the masculine plural `תַּחֲלֻאִים` the relative modifies, and leaves the `בְּ` `unrepresented` under rule 40, since the ASV promotes its object to the direct object of *made ... sick*. A relative left holding such a word by itself is not a unit short of its parts: the corpus aligns a bare `אֲשֶׁר` to *wherewith* in fifty-five units, and its *wherein* units include bare relatives beside the three-morpheme fusions. Count the English pronouns against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s: where the ASV writes a pronoun besides the adverb, some morpheme other than the relative answers for it, and where it writes none, the resumption is inside the adverb and the paragraphs above govern. **A distributive repetition is read on those same terms, and there the rendered occurrence is the first.** Where Hebrew joins a noun to a repetition of itself with a waw and the ASV writes one English noun with a distributive determiner standing before it — `לְשַׁעַר וָשָׁעַר` → *at* ***every gate***, and likewise *each* or *every one* — the first occurrence takes the noun's own English word together with that supplied determiner under rule 15, the waw is `unrepresented` under rule 14 for want of a written connective, and the repeated occurrence is `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence. Do not fuse the three morphemes into one unit under rule 30: that rule's condition is one rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and the English noun is a word the ASV spends on this noun in particular, which the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use finds gone with it while the repetition and the coordination are left saying nothing either way. Tail-to-tail above governs a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral and does not reach this: what the ASV writes here is a determiner and a noun opening one phrase, and the first occurrence is where they stand, exactly as rule 47 reads a phrase's single *the* onto the first of the articles it opens. Three limits. Where a single English word carries the whole repetition, spending nothing on either occurrence in particular — a lone adverb such as *daily* — rule 30's condition is met and the morphemes share one unit as before. Where the ASV writes a connective for the waw, or an English word for each occurrence, nothing is left unrendered, rule 2 splits them, and each morpheme takes the word written for it. And where an article or another determiner morpheme stands on the noun, that morpheme takes the written determiner under rules 41 and 15 as it always does, since what this paragraph places is the repetition and not the determiner.
amendments.why: 2CH.35.15 rendered לְשַׁעַר וָשָׁעַר as at every gate, and the verse pass had to reverse an earlier reading that fused the noun, its waw and the repeated noun into one rule 30 unit. The contract had no sentence on the distributive repetition, so the division had to be assembled from rules 14, 15, 22 and 30 each time, and rule 22's own tail-to-tail sentence pointed the wrong way because it was written for a counted noun in a compound numeral. The amendment states the division and its ground (the noun's English word is spent on one morpheme in particular, so rule 30's condition fails), and keeps rule 30 for a one-word rendering such as daily and rule 2 for a rendering that writes a word for each occurrence. Nothing in the corpus supplied here bears against it: the only unit of this shape in the searched material is the one this chapter aligned, and the reasoning is rule 30's own subtraction test.

conventions: In ka- plus the assimilated article plus the passive participle katuv, the substantival article takes whichever pronoun the ASV writes in that slot and heads on it under rule 41, while the participle keeps the supplied copula and the lexical verb: 35.12 as it is written gives it to the article and is written to the participle, and 35.26 according to that which is written gives that which the same way. Rule 20's ruling that an impersonal it is added does not reach it, because a present article morpheme licenses the pronoun (rule 11); the finished corpus reads the same assimilated article as it at 2CH.30.5 and 2CH.30.18, both kakkatuv.

Where the ASV completes a compound numeral figure with a counted noun the Hebrew does not write (the italic small cattle at 35.8 and 35.9), that supplied noun joins the closing numeral's unit and the head stays on the numeral (rule 31), tail to tail with rule 22's reading of a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral. Joining it to the opening numeral was the competing reading and is recorded here so that later figures in the book divide the same way; where the Hebrew does write the counted noun, as with baqar in the second figure of each verse, that noun is its own unit as usual.

Tail-to-tail above governs a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral and does not reach this: what the ASV writes here is a determiner and a noun opening one phrase, and the first occurrence is where they stand, exactly as rule 47 reads a phrase's single *the* onto the first of the articles it opens. Three limits. Where a single English word carries the whole repetition, spending nothing on either occurrence in particular — a lone adverb such as *daily* — rule 30's condition is met and the morphemes share one unit as before. Where the ASV writes a connective for the waw, or an English word for each occurrence, nothing is left unrendered, rule 2 splits them, and each morpheme takes the word written for it. And where an article or another determiner morpheme stands on the noun, that morpheme takes the written determiner under rules 41 and 15 as it always does, since what this paragraph places is the repetition and not the determiner.
amended.why: 2CH.35.15 rendered לְשַׁעַר וָשָׁעַר as at every gate, and the verse pass had to reverse an earlier reading that fused the noun, its waw and the repeated noun into one rule 30 unit. The contract had no sentence on the distributive repetition, so the division had to be assembled from rules 14, 15, 22 and 30 each time, and rule 22's own tail-to-tail sentence pointed the wrong way because it was written for a counted noun in a compound numeral. The amendment states the division and its ground (the noun's English word is spent on one morpheme in particular, so rule 30's condition fails), and keeps rule 30 for a one-word rendering such as daily and rule 2 for a rendering that writes a word for each occurrence. Nothing in the corpus supplied here bears against it: the only unit of this shape in the searched material is the one this chapter aligned, and the reasoning is rule 30's own subtraction test.

report: Checked all 58 candidate lemma groups, then read the 27-verse dump end to end for the asymmetries the table is blind to (added units, and English folded into a licensing morpheme in one verse but marked added in another). No genuine split found; patches is empty.

Determiner counting is uniform and follows rules 29 and 41 as a count of the ASV's own words: an article on a rectum takes the single written the where the rectum is rendered anarthrously (35.8 the house of God, 35.16 the commandment of king Josiah, 35.17 the feast of unleavened bread, and attributively at 35.3 and 35.24); it takes the determiner standing before the possessor where the chain is recast as an English possessive (35.7, 35.10, 35.15, and the supplied a of 35.5 a father's house); and it is unrepresented where another morpheme answers for the phrase's one determiner (35.3 and 35.27 a suffix, 35.17 and 35.19 a demonstrative pronoun). 35.16 the same day writes two determiners, so each morpheme takes the one standing before its own word, while 35.17 at that time writes one and the pronoun takes it. That is rule 41's count, not a split.

Numerals are equally licensed by the source: 35.1 the fourteenth day and 35.8/35.9 small cattle complete substantival numerals for which the Hebrew writes no counted noun (rules 15, 31), whereas 35.19 the eighteenth year puts the supplied the on the written shanah. Supplied object pronouns run both ways consistently: added where no suffix stands (35.11 them after flayed, 35.13 them after carried), aligned where one does (35.24, 35.25).

The two treatments of the assimilated article on kakkatuv are one analysis, not two: 35.12 gives it the it of as it is written and 35.26 the that which of according to that which is written, both under rule 41, with the participle keeping is written in each. The corpus reads [ha] as it in eight units, including 2CH.30.5 and 2CH.30.18, which are this same construction in this same book, so rule 20's added impersonal it does not reach it. Recorded as a convention.

All eight added units are English no morpheme licenses (35.3 more, 35.5 for each, 35.11 the blood which they received and them, 35.13 them, 35.14 busied, 35.21 I come and meddling with). None duplicates a word that elsewhere in the chapter was folded into a licensing morpheme.

BSB: 20 disagreements over 700 comparable occurrences, and none is a genuine error. Td x 9 and R x 6 are the documented convention families (an article for which the ASV writes no the, rule 29; a preposition the ASV's recasting leaves nothing to say, rules 27 and 40). The remainder are the same conventions one token at a time: 35.15 and 35.21 waws for which the ASV writes no connective, 35.15 the repeated shaar of every gate (rule 22), 35.16 ba before the bare adverbial the same day (rule 40), and 35.21 attah, whose thee the suffix on alav already holds (rules 22, 25). No accepted edge was changed.

One amendment, to rule 22: 35.15 leshaar washaar rendered at every gate is a distributive repetition the contract nowhere addresses, and the verse pass had to reverse a three-morpheme rule 30 fusion to get it right. The amendment states the division (first occurrence takes the noun and the supplied determiner, the waw and the repeated occurrence go unrepresented) and keeps rule 30 for a one-word rendering such as daily.
